content: 1. For women in the post-abortion period who require contraception, the administration of injectable contraceptives by traditional and complementary medicine professionals, pharmacy workers, or community health workers is being evaluated as a safe, effective, and acceptable alternative to provision by trained health workers. The outcomes assessed include contraceptive uptake and continuation, safety (serious adverse events and complications), effectiveness (method failure), and satisfaction or acceptability. 2. For pregnant individuals seeking medical abortion, the provision of medical abortion care through telemedicine, either as comprehensive care or as individual components (e.g., eligibility assessment, counseling, instructions, facilitation, and follow-up), is being assessed as a safe, effective, and acceptable alternative to in-person medical abortion care. Outcomes include effectiveness (rates of ongoing pregnancy, success of abortion without surgical intervention, and need for surgical evacuation), safety (serious adverse events and complications), satisfaction or acceptability, adherence to recommended dose regimens, and reported cost of services. 3. For pregnant individuals seeking induced abortion, community-based outreach models involving health workers are being evaluated as safe, effective, and acceptable alternatives to abortion care provided in a healthcare facility by trained health workers. Outcomes include safety (serious adverse events and complications), effectiveness (success of abortion without surgical intervention), cost-effectiveness, increased health-seeking behaviors, and satisfaction or acceptability. This is particularly relevant in settings with weak infrastructure or legally restrictive environments. 4. For pregnant individuals seeking induced abortion, harm-reduction counseling on abortion care is being assessed as a safe, effective, and acceptable alternative to routine in-clinic service delivery. Outcomes include safety (serious adverse events and complications), effectiveness (success of abortion without surgical intervention), and satisfaction or acceptability. This approach is being considered in both humanitarian and non-humanitarian settings. 5. For pregnant individuals seeking induced abortion, social marketing outreach methods are being evaluated for their ability to improve access to safe, effective, and acceptable abortion services compared to in-clinic abortion care provided by trained health workers. Outcomes include safety (serious adverse events and complications), effectiveness (success of abortion without surgical intervention), access (affordability, utilization, client volume, attendance, and coverage), quality of care (abortion methods of choice, quality of information provided, provider competence, and provider-patient relationship), adverse effects (undesirable impacts on existing services or inappropriate use of services), equitable access or utilization, cost of services, and satisfaction or acceptability. 6. For pregnant individuals seeking induced abortion, self-sourcing of medications through online sources without a prescription is being assessed as a safe, effective, and acceptable alternative to obtaining a prescription and/or medications from a trained health worker. Outcomes include safety (serious adverse events and complications), effectiveness (success of abortion without surgical intervention), quality of medications, and satisfaction or acceptability. 7. For individuals in the post-abortion period who require contraception, self-administration of injectable contraceptives (either initiation or continuation) is being evaluated as a safe, effective, and acceptable alternative to provision by trained health workers. Outcomes include contraceptive uptake and continuation, safety (serious adverse events and complications related to the method), effectiveness (method failure), and satisfaction or acceptability. 8. The WHO guideline on abortion care will be disseminated digitally (interactive web-based version and downloadable PDF) and in print. It will also be included in the annually updated compendium of WHO-approved recommendations. Dissemination will occur through NGO partners, professional association websites, and social media platforms. Print versions will be distributed to WHO regional and country offices, NGO partners, and professional associations. Translations into Spanish, French, Portuguese, and other UN languages are planned, with third-party translations encouraged under WHO guidance. 9. The guideline will be launched through regional dissemination meetings, knowledge transfer activities, and implementation research in select countries. Additional products, such as PowerPoint presentations summarizing key messages and evidence, and social media materials, will support the launch. WHO regional offices and NGO partners will play active roles in dissemination and adaptation. 10. The guideline will be presented online in an interactive web-based format shortly after the publication of the standard version, allowing it to function as a living guideline. This format will enable continuous review of new research evidence, updates to recommendations, and the inclusion of new topics as needed. A database system is being developed to facilitate ongoing evidence review and inform future updates. 11. The guideline consolidates and updates recommendations from three previous WHO guidelines on abortion care. Future updates will address new topics as required. The rapidly evolving nature of interventions and approaches for quality abortion care, particularly self-management, necessitates continuous literature review. Systematic reviews will be updated as needed, and new questions will undergo evidence retrieval, synthesis, and application of the GRADE approach in line with WHO standards. 12. All technical products developed during the guideline process, including systematic review reports, search strategies, and search dates, will be archived for future reference. Concerns about the validity of recommendations based on new evidence will prompt updates to systematic reviews. The original search strategy will be reapplied, and new questions will follow the same rigorous process for evidence evaluation and recommendation development.
